source.title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution

accepted.question_text: What galaxy-scale star-formation law should semi-analytic galaxy-formation models use so that they can reproduce observed galaxy populations across stellar mass, redshift, clustering, specific star-formation rate, and gas content? In this setting, semi-analytic models follow galaxy formation on dark-matter merger trees and include gas cooling, star formation, feedback, and merging. Standard prescriptions often use a Kennicutt-Schmidt-like law in which the star-formation rate is roughly proportional to cold gas mass, inversely proportional to a galactic-disk timescale, and cut off below a sharp low-gas-density threshold. The unresolved problem is to determine whether a successful law should remove the sharp cold-gas threshold, depend more strongly on host halo mass, have weak or no dependence on cosmic time, depend on molecular rather than total cold gas, and/or use a lower high-redshift normalization, while remaining physically plausible and observationally successful.
accepted.context_brief: Galaxy-scale star-formation law in semi-analytic models

evidence.quote:
This simple SF law is however likely an oversim-
pliﬁcation. In recent years observational determinations
of the SF law in galaxies have become increasingly re-
ﬁned, using various gas components (HI, CO) in com-
bination with more reliable estimates of SF, based on
UV and IR light.

It is also not clear which
gas mass correlates best with the SF rate when aver-
aging over the entire galaxy (e.g. Saintonge et al. 2011).
Third, there are both theoretical and observational indi-
cations that the normalization of the SF law might be
lower at high redshift than locally

We instead try to solve in
a straightforward way the inverse problem, namely which
realistic SF law at galactic scales is required to improve
the agreement between model galaxies and observations.

accepted.question_text: Can a single high-resolution semi-analytic model of galaxy formation simultaneously match the observed specific-star-formation-rate--stellar-mass relation at redshift z = 0, the stellar mass function and its evolution, galaxy two-point correlation functions, and galaxy cold-gas fractions? The model must do this without relying on unrestricted tuning of all physical recipes and while keeping its star-formation, feedback, cooling, and merging prescriptions physically plausible.

evidence.quote:
Up to now, a high-resolution SAM that matches
the SSFR-stellar mass relation at z = 0, the SMF and
its evolution, the correlation functions and the cold gas
fractions of galaxies simultaneously, does not yet seem to
exist.

These results show again that
it is currently diﬃcult for a single model to ﬁt all observa-
tions, as mentioned in Sec. 1, unless we allow for free tuning
of all recipes, including cooling (see NW2010).

accepted.question_text: How can semi-analytic galaxy-formation models reproduce the low-mass end of the stellar mass function without creating other failures, such as too little star formation in low-mass galaxies at z = 0, too many red low-mass galaxies, excessive stellar mass functions at redshifts 0.8 to 2.5, overly high galaxy auto-correlation functions, physically hard-to-motivate supernova feedback efficiencies, or a dramatic overprediction of the cold gas content of galaxies? The open task is to find a physically motivated combination of star-formation, supernova-feedback, gas-cooling, and gas-heating or gas-expulsion prescriptions that resolves these linked constraints together.
accepted.context_brief: Low-mass stellar mass function without compensating failures

evidence.quote:
In order to reproduce the low mass end of the stellar mass function , most cur-
rent models of galaxy evolution invoke very eﬃcient supernova feed back. This solution
seems to suﬀer from several shortcomings however, like predictin g too little star for-
mation in low mass galaxies at z=0.

However, they also predict a too
large fraction of red galaxies at low masses, too high ampli-
tudes of the stellar mass functions in the redshift range of
[0.8, 2.5], and galaxy auto-correlation functions that are too
high for galaxies less massive than 6 × 1010M⊙ . Moreover,
the high feedback eﬃciency as used by Guo et al. (2011)
is physically diﬃcult to motivate

However, our modiﬁcations also lead to a dramatic overpred iction of the cold
mass content of galaxies. This shows that ﬁnding a successful mod el may require ﬁne-
tuning of both star formation and supernovae feedback, as well a s improvements on
gas cooling, or perhaps the inclusion of a yet unknown process which eﬃciently heats
or expels gas at high redshifts.

accepted.question_text: When semi-analytic galaxy-formation models fail to match observed galaxy two-point auto-correlation functions, is the mismatch primarily caused by the baryonic recipes used to assign stellar masses and galaxy properties, or by the underlying cosmology of the dark-matter simulation? The issue is nontrivial because galaxy positions are tied to haloes and subhaloes, while stellar-mass selection and clustering predictions can change substantially when the star-formation law changes, and similar clustering matches can be obtained with different cosmological parameters depending on the baryonic recipes.
accepted.context_brief: Baryonic recipes versus cosmology in galaxy clustering

evidence.quote:
The two point auto-correlation function of galaxies is a fun -
damental measure of the spatial distribution of a certain
population of galaxies and is well determined by observa-
tions (e.g. Li et al. 2006). It is however not well ﬁtted by
current SAMs.

Thus, it is in general very hard to say
whether a mismatch with observed correlation functions in-
dicates a problem with baryonic recipes, or with cosmology.

We thus conﬁrm the results by Wang et al. (2008) who ﬁnd
that a similar match to observed correlation functions can b e
obtained by SAMs using diﬀerent cosmological parameters,
depending on the detailed baryonic recipes.

accepted.question_text: Is it necessary and physically justified for the star-formation efficiency in semi-analytic galaxy-formation models to have weak or no dependence on cosmic time? In the model family considered here, removing the usual time dependence of the star-formation rate may improve some observables, but it is unclear whether that modification is required and what physical mechanism, such as a time-dependent conversion of atomic to molecular gas, would produce the opposite time scaling from standard assumptions.

evidence.quote:
Results of model 3b) are similar to model 3) out to
z ∼ 2, except that the SSFR– Mstar relation is slightly less
well reproduced. It is thus not clear whether modiﬁcation
iii) is necessary.

In order to justify the behaviour we suggest in model 3), we
would need to postulate a mechanism that scales with time
in the opposite way than usually assumed, like for example a
metallicity-dependent conversion of atomic to molecular g as
(Krumholz & Dekel 2011).

We note that a weak dependence
of the SF eﬃciency on cosmic time was seen in hydrodynam-
ical simulations (Neistein et al. 2011b), although the reas on
for this behaviour is still not clear.

accepted.question_text: What missing baryonic physical process or corrected cooling prescription, if any, prevents semi-analytic galaxy-formation models from overproducing cold gas while preserving successful fits to stellar masses, star-formation rates, and clustering? Candidate directions include preheating gas so that it cannot cool into low-mass haloes, feedback that preferentially heats low-entropy gas in high-redshift haloes, and revised gas-cooling treatments, but the unresolved task is to identify a process that is physically plausible and works simultaneously with the other galaxy observables.
accepted.context_brief: Cold-gas overproduction and missing baryonic physics

evidence.quote:
Although there are some uncertainties related to the
determination of cold gas mass function in observation
(Keres et al. 2003; Obreschkow & Rawlings 2009; Fu et al.
2010), it seems that our models with modiﬁed SF predict
drastically too much cold gas mass in galaxies.

It is not clear up to now if
this diﬃculty in modeling galaxy properties reﬂects a fun-
damental problem in our understanding of the dark matter
universe, or if it is mainly due to an insuﬃcient understand-
ing of the baryonic physics involved in galaxy formation and
evolution.

For example, perhaps SAMs miss an important in-
gredient of galaxy formation, like a mechanism that preheat s
the gas in the universe so that it cannot cool to low mass
haloes (Mo et al. 2005, but see also Crain et al. (2007)), or
a form of feedback that mainly heats low entropy gas in
high redshift haloes (McCarthy et al. 2011). Alternatively ,
it could be that cooling is over-eﬃcient in the current SAMs
for some reason.
